claims.claim: The risk score is based on a comprehensive analysis of five key factors. The first factor is hidden fees and pricing risks, which evaluates whether the contract contains undisclosed charges, inflated markups, administrative surcharges, or pricing terms that could cost you significantly more than the stated price. The second factor is one-sided clauses and liability issues, which identifies terms that give disproportionate advantage to one party, such as unlimited liability waivers, unilateral modification rights, or mandatory arbitration clauses that limit your legal recourse. The third factor is scope and definition clarity, assessing whether the contract clearly defines what each party is responsible for or uses vague language that could be interpreted in multiple ways. The fourth factor is payment term fairness, evaluating the schedule, conditions, and consequences of payment. The fifth factor is termination and renewal terms, identifying automatic renewal clauses, excessive cancellation penalties, and locked-in pricing that could become unfavorable over time.

claims.claim: One of the most powerful concepts in hidden fee intelligence is understanding the difference between legitimate charges and hidden fees. Not every charge on your bill is a hidden fee. A charge that is buried in fine print, described in vague terms, or added without your knowledge or consent is a hidden fee, and it is worth challenging. claims.claim: Set a recurring calendar reminder to review every bank statement, credit card statement, utility bill, and subscription charge each month. Look for fees that appeared without notification, price increases on services you use regularly, equipment rental charges that exceed the purchase cost of the equipment, regulatory fees that are not actual government taxes, and duplicate charges for the same service. Catching these fees within the first billing cycle gives you the strongest position for having them removed. Many companies will waive fees discovered within 30-60 days but require more documentation for older charges.

claims.claim: Maintain a spreadsheet of every active subscription including the start date, promotional rate, standard rate, renewal date, and cancellation requirements. Set calendar alerts 7 days before each renewal date to evaluate whether you still use and need the service. The average consumer pays for 3-5 subscriptions they no longer use, totaling $300-$800 annually in wasted charges. Use virtual credit card numbers for free trials so they expire automatically when the trial period ends.

claims.claim: Subscriptions are designed to be forgotten. Companies that offer subscription services count on a certain percentage of customers continuing to pay month after month for services they no longer use or even remember signing up for. Auto-renewal clauses are the primary mechanism that makes this possible. Most subscription agreements include terms that automatically renew your subscription at the end of each billing period unless you take specific action to cancel before the renewal date. Some companies make cancellation intentionally difficult by requiring phone calls during limited business hours, not providing confirmation of cancellation, or requiring multiple steps to complete the process. Free trial conversions are one of the most common subscription traps. You sign up for a free trial of a service, intending to cancel before the trial period ends, but you forget to cancel and your credit card is charged the full subscription price. Some companies make it particularly difficult to cancel during the trial period, requiring you to call and speak with a retention specialist who will try to convince you to stay. Price increases on existing subscriptions are another hidden cost. Many subscription services reserve the right to increase prices at any time with minimal notice to existing customers. You may be paying a higher price for months or years without realizing the rate has increased because the charge is automatically deducted from your account each month. Add-on subscriptions that are bundled with main services, forgotten subscriptions from years ago that continue charging your credit card, and subscriptions that continue after you have stopped using the service all contribute to the growing problem of subscription creep. Review your bank and credit card statements every month specifically looking for recurring charges you no longer need or want. Cancel any subscriptions you are not actively using and consider using a subscription management service to track all of your recurring expenses in one place.
